title: MB8-11630
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The appellant, XXXX XXXX, a Haitian citizen, is appealing against the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision rejecting his refugee protection claim on the grounds that he was not credible when he alleged that he fears for his life in Haiti.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellant, XXXX XXXX, a Haitian citizen, is appealing against the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision rejecting his refugee protection claim on the grounds that he was not credible when he alleged that he fears for his life in Haiti. The appellant argues that the RPD's findings do not take into account the evidence filed in support of his testimony. The appeal is dismissed. The evidence does not establish that the appellant still faces a serious possibility of persecution by reason of his imputed political opinion.

In 2015, based on the allegations in the appellant's refugee protection claim,1 he was the senior supervisor at a polling station in XXXX during two rounds of the municipal and presidential elections. Supporters of the team that ran the municipality were unhappy that he was chosen for the position because the appellant had previously publicly criticized municipal management and because his brother was a mayoral candidate in that election. As the votes were counted, the appellant was subjected to acts of intimidation, which went on for several months. For his own safety, the appellant felt that he had to leave XXXX, but he remained in Haiti until April 2016. The appellant travelled to the United States, but he returned to Haiti voluntarily on XXXX XXXX, 2016, because his American visa had expired.

He and his spouse then moved to XXXX. Two weeks after they arrived, they attended a meeting organized by a group of young professionals, and the topic of sexual orientation was discussed. The appellant expressed his support for holding a festival promoting freedom of choice for sexual orientation. That caused an uproar among those in attendance, and the appellant and his spouse felt that they should leave the meeting.

Eight months later, on June 15, 2017, while the appellant was attending a soccer game, two people stopped him and started shoving and hitting him, criticizing him for promoting homosexuality. They left when some police officers approached. The appellant claimed that this incident made him realize that he would not be safe in Haiti. He therefore left the country two months later, on XXXX XXXX, 2017, and came to Canada via the United States.

The RPD found that the appellant's allegations were not credible.2 Although the RPD acknowledged that the appellant had filed an attestation from a justice of the peace3 confirming that had suffered [translation] "serious persecution" due to his role as the supervisor at a polling station, the RPD stated that it could not give probative value to the attestation because it did not specify how the appellant had been persecuted and because he did not file the complaints to which the attestation referred. Moreover, the RPD concluded that the appellant's decision to return to Haiti in October 2016 showed that he no longer had any fear stemming from the events connected to the 2015 elections. Regarding the appellant's support for holding a festival promoting freedom of choice for sexual orientation, the RPD stated that he could not claim refugee status on that basis because he was not identified as a sexual minorities rights advocate.

In his memorandum of appeal,4 the appellant argues that the RPD should have acknowledged that the attestation from the justice of the peace establishes that he had been persecuted in 2015-2016. Moreover, the appellant considers that the RPD was wrong when it stated that his return to Haiti in October 2016 signalled that he no longer feared for his safety. He argues that his brother's political involvement and his own imputed political involvement with the LGBTI community continue to make him a political target in Haiti.

The appellant is also asking to present new evidence, namely, an article from a French journal, Mariane, dated August 3, 2017, titled "Haÿti : Le SÕnat vote une loi instituant une homophobie d'ètat" [Haiti: the senate passes a law instituting state-wide homophobia].5 ADMISSIBILITY OF NEW EVIDENCE

I find that the appellant did not demonstrate that the new evidence presented on appeal meets the test for admissibility set out in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA. To be admissible, the evidence must have arisen after the refugee protection claim was rejected by the RPD or must not have been reasonably available at that time. However, the claim was rejected on April 27, 2018, more than eight months after the publication of the article that the appellant would like to file into evidence in the appeal. The appellant does not explain, in either his written statement or his memorandum of appeal, why he could not reasonably have been expected to present this evidence to the RPD, despite the obligation to do so under subparagraph 3(3)(g)(iii) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules.

To determine whether the appeal is well founded, the following questions must be answered: * Did the RPD err by concluding that the appellant does not face a serious possibility of persecution by reason of his duties during the 2015 elections? * Did the RPD err by concluding that the appellant does not face a serious possibility of persecution by reason of his support for holding a festival promoting freedom of choice for sexual orientation?

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) reviews RPD decisions by applying the correctness standard, after carrying out its own analysis of the record. The exception to that rule concerns RPD findings when assessing the credibility or weight to be given to the oral testimony it hears, in situations where it enjoys a meaningful advantage.

In this case, I find that there are no RPD findings for which it enjoyed a meaningful advantage. Consequently, I only applied the correctness standard. MERITS OF THE APPEAL Appellant's failure to claim asylum in the United States

The appellant is challenging the RPD's finding that his failure to claim asylum in the United States during his stay there in 2016 undermines his credibility. In my opinion, that finding is wrong. The appellant was in the United States for less than five months, and he had a visitor's visa allowing him to stay there legally for four months, virtually the entire time he was there. It is reasonable that he did not start the process to be recognized as a refugee at that time, because he was in the country legally. His credibility is not undermined. Evidence of the appellant's involvement in the 2015 elections

I have read the attestation dated July 25, 2017, which was issued by a justice of the peace from the peace court of XXXX. This document, in addition to mentioning "serious persecution" against the appellant following the 2015 elections, also indicates that members of the PHTK party had conspired to kill him [translation] "even before the last elections were held." However, the document does not mention that the acts of persecution against the appellant continued beyond January 27, 2016, the date given as the date of the most recent complaint filed by the appellant, long before he returned to Haiti after his stay in the United States.

Therefore, I do not see how this attestation constitutes relevant evidence establishing that the persecution against the appellant in the past is likely to occur again should he now return to Haiti, four years after said elections. I agree with the RPD that the fact that the appellant felt sufficiently at ease to return to Haiti to live in October 2016, although not in the part of the country where he had lived before, shows that, at the time, he believed that there was no reason to fear that the persecution against him would resume. Moreover, by his own admission, during the ensuing 10 months when he lived in that location, the role he played during the 2015 elections did not cause him any problems. Evidence of the appellant's support for holding a festival promoting freedom of choice for sexual orientation

The appellant mentioned only one incident that he blamed on an opinion expressed during a meeting in mid-October 2016, and that incident only occurred eight months later. In my opinion, it was a relatively minor incident, which the appellant did not even bother to report to the police who were present. Moreover, the incident did not prevent him from remaining in XXXX for another two months. That is why the appellant is not credible when he claims that it was that incident that prompted his move to Canada.

The RPD's findings on the appellant's credibility are well founded. He did not demonstrate that he would face a serious possibility of persecution by reason of his imputed political opinion. He also failed to demonstrate that he would likely be subjected to a risk to his life or to cruel and unusual treatment by reason of any other ground. Accordingly, the appellant is not a refugee or a person in need of protection.

Consequently, the appeal is dismissed.
